newsitem.title: USA: U.S., North Korea discussing submarine incident.
newsitem.headline: U.S., North Korea discussing submarine incident.

text.p: U.S. and North Korean diplomats plan to meet again in New York soon in a drive to patch up the damage from the North's submarine incursion into South Korean waters, State Department officials said on Thursday.

The officials said one or more additional meetings may take place as they press North Korea to make a statement about the Sept. 18 submarine incident "that satisfies" the South. Previous working-level meetings took place on Saturday and Monday.
The submarine incident, in which 26 North Korean commandos went ashore, infuriated Seoul, which put relations with the North into a deep freeze pending an apology.
"The talks continue to be serious and useful, but we really don't want to characterise them beyond that," a State Department spokesman said.

John Dinger, another spokesman, told reporters Li Hyong Chol, director of American affairs in North Korea's Foreign Ministry, had not set a date to leave New York. "We continue to believe that there may be additional sessions in New York," Dinger said.

Mark Minton, director of the State Department's office of Korean affairs, has been leading the U.S. side. The North Korean delegation to the United Nations did not return a phone call seeking comment.

An official who spoke on condition he not be named said the top immediate U.S. goal was resolution of the submarine incident. This would clear the way for progress on four-party talks proposed by the United States and South Korea with the North and China on a lasting peace to replace the truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.

It would also clear the way for further discussion of the proposed opening of a U.S. diplomatic liasion office in Pyongyang, which has been bogged down over technical details, and would set the stage for further implementation of the U.S.-brokered 1994 deal under which the North abandoned its suspected nuclear weapons programme in exchange for safer nuclear reactors and shipments of fuel oil.
